about: Twenty laws on striking and wounding: the stele’s “eye for an eye” block. A son who strikes his father has his hand cut off (§195; whether one hand or two is uncertain). Between men of the same rank the penalty is the injury itself: the eye destroyed, the bone broken, the tooth knocked out are repaid in kind (§196, §197, §200); but when the injured man is a commoner or a man’s slave the code asks silver instead (§198–199, §201). The blow to the face follows: a man who strikes the cheek of one greater than himself is flogged sixty strokes with an ox-hide whip in the assembly (§202); between equals the fine is one mina, between commoners ten shekels (§203–204); a slave who strikes a man’s son loses an ear (§205). Then the brawl: a man who wounds another in a quarrel swears that he did not do it knowingly and pays the physician (§206); if the man dies of the blow he swears and pays half a mina (for a man’s son) or a third of a mina (for a commoner’s son) (§207–208). The last six laws are about a pregnant woman struck so that she loses her child: ten shekels for a man’s daughter, five for a commoner’s, two for a slave-woman (§209, §211, §213); and if the woman herself dies, the striker’s own daughter is put to death (§210), or silver is paid, half a mina for a commoner’s daughter and a third of a mina for a slave-woman (§212, §214). The penalties are exactly as the stele states them. A few words (the two verbs of the eye clause, “cheek”, “brawl”, the two signs for “hand”, the sign group for “whip”) cannot be read with certainty; the notes say so each time.

sentences.i: If a son has struck his father,
sentences.n: The first of twenty laws on blows and wounds. §195–200 are the laws of the hand, the eye, the bone and the tooth (repaid in kind between equals, in silver otherwise), §201–205 the fines for a tooth and for a blow to the face, §206–208 the brawl, §209–214 the blow that makes a woman lose her child. Each is one “if” sentence, cut here at its verbs. šumma mārum abašu imtaḫaṣ is “if a-son his-father has-struck”: mārum is “son”, written with the single sign DUMU (Harper prints the ending -um, no ending is written on the plate); abašu is abum “father” in the accusative (-a-) with -šu “his”; imtaḫaṣ is the perfect (the infixed -ta-) of maḫāṣum “to strike”, the tense the code uses for a completed act in its “if” clause: “has struck”. The last sign of imtaḫaṣ is the AZ sign read aṣ, as everywhere in this part.

sentences.i: they shall cut off his hands.
sentences.n: The apodosis (the penalty): rittēšu inakkisū is “his-hands they-shall-cut-off”. inakkisū is the present, 3rd person plural, of nakāsum “to cut (off)”, with the plural ending -ū (written i-na-ak-ki-su, final sign SU as Harper prints it); a plural verb with no subject word is an impersonal “they”: the code does not say who does it, and the same form carries the penalties that follow (“they shall cut off”). rittēšu is two signs, UM and a vertical-and-bar sign that I key ME, then ŠU for -šu “his”; Harper’s list no. 65 gives UM + that sign as rittu “hand” and he normalizes rit-tê-šu. On the plate the second sign is a vertical wedge with a horizontal tail, the shape of his no. 184 me (his no. 181 lal is drawn alike), and his rittu entry shows UM followed by the same shape. The identification of the second sign is UNCERTAIN, and so is the number: -ē is a plural/dual ending in Harper’s normalization (“hands”); a single hand is possible. The penalty fits the offence: the hand that struck the father.

sentences.i: If a man has destroyed the eye of a man’s son,
sentences.n: §196, the most quoted law of the code. The talion laws are rendered from the grammar alone, and the same pattern runs through §196–200: a protasis with the perfect (“has done X to …”) and an apodosis with the present plural (“they shall do X to him”). šumma awīlum īn mār awīlim uḫtabbit is “if a-man the-eye-of a-man’s-son has-destroyed”. īn is īnum “eye” in the construct state (no ending, because a genitive follows), spelled i-in; mār awīlim is “a man’s son”, DUMU with the genitive awīlim: a member of the awīlum class, the code’s first rank. uḫtabbit is the perfect of the D-stem (the intensive; the u- is its mark) of ḫabātum, whose dictionary sense is “to rob, plunder”; “has destroyed” is taken from the sense of the law (the eye is lost), not derived from the grammar, which shows only an intensive of a verb of robbing. That it means “blinded” is likewise the sense of the law, not of the verb; the next unit puts the same eye on the offender. UNCERTAIN as a word.

sentences.i: they shall destroy his eye.
sentences.n: The talion itself: īnšu uḫappadū is “his-eye they-shall-destroy”. īnšu is īnum with -šu “his”; uḫappadū is a D-stem present, 3rd plural, of a verb ḫapādum, with the plural ending -ū. That verb is not met elsewhere in the code and I cannot confirm its meaning from the grammar; the sense “destroy” is taken from the law, where it must answer uḫtabbit above: the offender’s own eye is taken. The Akkadian has two different verbs (ḫabātum-D above, ḫapādum-D here); English “destroy” stands for both because the grammar does not tell them apart. UNCERTAIN as a word, plain as a law. House rendering of the pair: īn mār awīlim uḫtabbit … īnšu uḫappadū “has destroyed the eye of a man’s son … they shall destroy his eye”.

sentences.i: If he has broken a man’s bone,
sentences.n: §197, the bone. The law has no subject word (“he” is understood from §196). NER.PAD.DU is a three-sign Sumerogram: NER (Harper’s reading of the foot sign; modern editions read it GÌR), PAD, and DU; it stands for “bone”, Akkadian eṣemtum. Harper writes the logogram as it stands and I read it as eṣemti, the construct state before the genitive awīlim, with the ending supplied (none is written): the exact Akkadian form is UNCERTAIN, the word is not. Harper’s list no. 170 draws NER.PAD.DU as these three signs together. ištebir is the perfect of šebērum “to break” (iš-te-bi-ir): “has broken”. On the plate awīlim stands on a second tier (Harper’s {b}).

sentences.i: If he has destroyed the eye of a commoner
sentences.n: §198: the same injuries to a commoner. MAŠ.EN.KAK is the Sumerogram (three signs, MAŠ, EN, KAK, no ending written) for muškēnum, the commoner, the code’s second rank; the case is read from the sentence: here muškēnim, the genitive after the construct īn. The law changes its penalty: where §196–197 repay an injury to a man’s son in kind, an injury to a commoner is paid in silver. The sentence is in two halves (eye, then bone), joined by u lū “or”.

sentences.i: he shall pay one mina of silver.
sentences.n: The penalty is a fine. išaqqal is the present of šaqālum “to weigh”, which is how silver is paid: “he shall pay”. The sum is ištēn mana kaspim, “one mina of silver”: the numeral is the single upright wedge DISH (said ištēn, “one”); mana is the mina (60 shekels, about half a kilogram) spelled with two syllable signs, ma-na (Harper prints ma-na in lower case; the plate shows two signs after the wedge); kaspim is kaspum “silver”, written KÙ.BABBAR: the two signs KÙ and BABBAR with no ending (on the plate only these two follow ma-na, here and in every silver line of this part); the -im of the genitive after mana is supplied by the grammar.

glossary.muškēnum: commoner, dependent freeman (MAŠ.EN.KAK) — the code’s second rank
glossary.mâtum: to die: imtūt (im-tu-ut, perfect) “he/she has died”, so ina šīmātīša imtūt “she died a natural death”
glossary.mārtum: daughter (written DUMU+ti): mārtišu “his daughter” · mārassu (DUMU.SAL-zu, three signs DUMU + SAL + ZU, ZU for -ssu) “his daughter” · mārtaka (DUMU.SAL-ka) “your daughter”, mārtī (DUMU.SAL-i) “my daughter”, mārtim (DUMU.SAL, no ending written) “of the daughter”: abī mārtim “the father of the daughter” · mārtišu also written DUMU.SAL-šu (DUMU + SAL + ŠU) “his daughter”: ana mārtišu “to his daughter” · mārat (DUMU.SAL, no ending written) construct “daughter of”: mārat awīlim “a man’s daughter”, mārat muškēnim “a commoner’s daughter”
glossary.mārum: son (DUMU) — here: a minor, not yet able to sell · member of a group: mārū ugārim (DUMU A.GÀR{meš}) “the sons of the irrigated land”, the district’s farmers · mār awīlim “a man’s son” (DUMU); mārī (DUMU{meš}) “sons” (oblique plural, which may include daughters, so “children”); māršu (DUMU-šu) “his son” · mārūša (DUMU{meš}-ša) “her sons” (nominative plural + suffix); mārīša (DUMU-ša) “her son” (genitive + suffix): ana mārīša “to her son” · mārī (DUMU-i) “my son” (-ī “my”); mārī (DUMU{meš}) “children” in mārī ūlissum “children she bore him”; mārū (DUMU{meš}) “sons” as subject: mārū ana ummātim ul izuzzū “the sons shall not divide by mothers” · mār X (DUMU, the sign TUR) “a member of the class X”, literally “son of X”: mār ummiānim “a craftsman”, mār zinništim “the son of a woman”; māram (DUMU) “a son”, mārašu (DUMU-šu) “his son”, mārī (DUMU{meš}) “sons”, mārīšu “his sons”
glossary.mēḫrum: equal, counterpart (one of the same rank): mēḫrišu (me-iḫ-ri-šu, with -šu) “his equal”, said of a man who stands level with the offender; the sense comes from the form and the law, matching ša kīma šuāti “who is like him” · noun
glossary.nadûm: to cast, throw (a charge; a body into the river): iddi, nadû, iddû · also to leave lying (a field): ittadi “he has left (it) lying” · of a flock: ṣēnī ana eqlim iddi “he turned the sheep loose into a field” · inaddûši (i-na-[ad]-du-u-ši) “they shall throw her” (present, plural, with -ši): ana mê inaddûši “they shall throw her into the water” · inaddûši “they shall throw him” of a man (§155, ana mê inaddûši), UNCERTAIN because the suffix -ši is “her” elsewhere · of a tooth, to knock out: ittadi (it-ta-di, perfect) “he has knocked out”, inaddû (i-na-ad-du-u, present plural) “they shall knock out”: šinni awīlim ittadi “he has knocked out a man’s tooth”
glossary.nadûm-Š: Š-stem of nadûm “to throw”: to make (someone) throw down, to strip of: uštaddišu (perfect, with -šu) “he made him throw (it) down” · make her drop, of a woman and what is in her womb: uštaddīši (uš-ta-di-ši, uš-ta-ad-di-ši, perfect, with -ši “her”) “he has made her drop”, i.e. made her miscarry; the geminate d is spelled once or twice
glossary.nakāsum: to cut, cut down: ikkis (preterite) “he cut down” · inakkisū (i-na-ak-ki-su) “they shall cut off”, present plural (the ending -sū is written with the one sign su, as Harper prints it): lišānšu inakkisū “they shall cut off his tongue”, tulêša inakkisū “they shall cut off her breast” · inakkisū “they shall cut off”, of the hand(s) and the ear: rittēšu inakkisū “they shall cut off his hand(s)”, uznašu inakkisū “they shall cut off his ear”
glossary.qinazum: whip, thong (the dictionary sense), UNCERTAIN: qinazi (genitive, after ina “with”) “with a whip”, written with the hide determinative {mašak} and the group qi₂-na-az; Harper lists the three pieces as one sign, so the split into syllables is a reconstruction and UNCERTAIN · noun, sense uncertain
glossary.rabûm: great; D/Š-stems “make great”; rabûtim “great (pl.)” · rabîtim (ra-bi-tim, feminine genitive) “large”: ina abnim rabîtim “by the large stone” · rabītišu (ra-bi-ti-šu) “his senior one”, the feminine with -šu: read as the father’s chief wife, UNCERTAIN
glossary.risbatum: brawl, quarrel (Harper’s sense), UNCERTAIN, the word is not met elsewhere: risbatim (ri-is-ba-tim, genitive after ina) “in a brawl” · noun, sense uncertain
glossary.rittum: hand: rittēšu (UM.ME-šu, the signs UM, ME and ŠU) “his hand(s)”, with -šu “his”; Harper normalizes rit-tê-šu with an ending -ê whose grammar is not clear to me; the second sign (read ME) and the number, one hand or two, are both UNCERTAIN · noun
glossary.tamûm: to swear (an oath): itamma (i-tam-ma, present, 3rd singular) “he shall swear”, itammama (i-tam-ma-ma) “he shall swear, and”, with -ma · verb
glossary.uznum: ear: uznašu (written u-zu-un-šu, with no vowel between un and šu; Harper normalizes accusative + -šu) “his ear”; the noun has no plural ending here, so one ear · noun
glossary.wardum: male slave (ARAD) · warad (ARAD, no ending written) “male slave of …”, wardam (ARAD-am)
glossary.zinništum: woman (written with the single sign SAL, ŠAL in Harper): zinništam, zinništim, zinništum
glossary.īnum: eye: īnšu … iššīma “he lifted his eye (to it)” — he coveted it · ša īnšu maḫru (i-in-šu) “whose eye is first” = the son he favours (UNCERTAIN idiom)
glossary.šakānum: to set, place: išakkanūšumma “they shall set for him (a term), and” · išakkanūšum (present, plural, dative -šum) “they shall place (it) for him”, i.e. count it to him · iššakkan (iš-ša-ak-ka-an, N-stem present) “it shall be put”: ul iššakkan “it shall not be put (in the account)” · to set, put, impose: ištakan (iš-ta-ka-an, perfect, “has set”), išakkan (present) — išakkanšima (i-ša-ak-ka-an-ši-ma, with -ši and -ma) “he/she shall set (it) on her, and”, as in abbuttam išakkan · išakkanūši “they shall set (her on a stake)”, išakkanūšumma “they shall set (it) aside for him, and” · idiom panam šakānum (panam ištakan) “to set the face” = to make up one’s mind · iššakkan also written iš-ta-ak-ka-an (Harper’s reading, UNCERTAIN): andurār amtim iššakkan “the release of the slave-woman shall be established”
glossary.šaqālum: to weigh out (silver = to pay): išqulu · išaqqal (present) “he shall weigh out”
glossary.šebērum: to break: ištebir (iš-te-bi-ir, perfect, 3rd singular) “he has broken”, išebbirū (i-še-ib-bi-ru, present, 3rd plural, with the b doubled) “they shall break” · verb
glossary.šinnum: tooth: šinni (ši-in-ni, construct) “the tooth of”, šinnašu (ši-in-na-šu, accusative + -šu) “his tooth” · noun
glossary.šiqlum: shekel — the basic weight of silver, about 8.3 g (written GÍN): 2 šiqil kaspim
glossary.šumma: if — the word that opens every law of the code
glossary.šuāti: that, the aforesaid · as the independent pronoun “him”: šuāti u bīšašu “him and his goods”
glossary.šī: she, that (feminine pronoun, as the independent word): ŠAL.GEŠ.TIN.NA šī “that tavern-keeper”; the masculine is šū
glossary.šīmum: purchase, purchase price · šīmišu (ŠÁM-šu, with -šu “his”) “his price”, of a slave: mišil šīmišu “half of his price”
glossary.šūši: sixty (written with the Sumerogram ŠU.ŠI, the signs ŠU and ŠI, preceded by the wedge 1): 1 šūši “sixty”; the thing counted (strokes) is not written · numeral
glossary.ḫabātum-D: UNCERTAIN verb, the D-stem (intensive) of ḫabātum “to rob, plunder”, taken here as “to destroy” from the sense of the law, not from the grammar: uḫtabbit (uḫ-tab-bi-it, perfect, 3rd singular) “he has destroyed (?)”, said of an eye · D-stem verb, sense uncertain
glossary.ḫapādum-D: UNCERTAIN verb, not met elsewhere in the code; D-stem present plural, read “to destroy” only because the law repays the offender with the same loss: uḫappadū (u-ḫa-ap-pa-du) “they shall destroy (?)”, said of the offender’s eye; the sense is UNCERTAIN · D-stem verb, sense uncertain
glossary.ṣimmum: wound (Harper’s sense), UNCERTAIN, not derivable from the grammar: ṣimmam (ṣi-im-ma-am, accusative) “a wound”; the first sign is the sign ZI in the autograph (Harper prints zi-im-ma-am here), read ṣi · noun, sense uncertain
